ranked_moves.title: A benchmark Polaris can lose: two plain-session arms (equal reach and full reach), frozen questions and a win rule fixed in advance
ranked_moves.relation: extends P7 (syzygy-fnry.7), which already plans a fresh reader answering frozen questions from the rendered site, and Q13's live scorecard (syzygy-3efd.57). New here: the plain-session arm, the blind grader with a key, the maintainer-documentation ceiling arm, the win rule fixed in advance, and one question file
ranked_moves.prereq: Owner decision, 2026-11-21, in the owner's words: asked what the plain-session arm may read and send, the owner chose 'Everything except detector matches' (the whole clone minus only files the secret detectors match; denied-path and active-content screens are dropped for this arm), over the recommended variant that kept those screens. It applies to this benchmark arm and to public repositories in R16's corpus only; it changes nothing about what a dossier run reads or sends, and no detector is weakened. The equal-reach arm needs no decision. Real runs come from R16's corpus runner after syzygy-k54o.3
ranked_moves.what: For each proving repository, three arms at the same pinned commit: the Polaris dossier; a plain session at equal reach (same model, the screened copy of the clone the author reads, a fixed published prompt and three fixed follow-ups, the same wall-time limit); a plain session at full reach, which is what a user would really get (the whole clone of a public corpus repository minus only the files the unchanged secret detectors match, as the owner decided on 2026-11-21); and the maintainers' own documentation as a ceiling. Before anything is generated, freeze one question file per repository shape: the reader questions, a depth list of ten to twenty non-obvious facts and trade-offs drawn from maintainer documents by a session that sees neither arm, and five reader tasks ('where would I change X'). Fresh readers answer from one arm only; a grader that is not told which arm it holds scores answers against the frozen key; forty sampled claims per arm are checked against the pinned tree. Both arms are shown to graders in the same neutral page shell. Record tokens, wall time and operator minutes for every arm. The win rule is written down first: Polaris wins only if its claim error rate is at most half the plain session's, its comprehension and depth scores are not more than ten percent lower, and its cost is within a stated multiple. Anything else is published as a loss, naming the dimension. The three question sets in the repository today (seven in TARGETS, five in the profile, four topics in the brief) become one versioned file that the brief, the reader test and the scorecard all read. Every published result names the arm it was won or lost against: a win at equal reach shows the mechanism helps; only a win at full reach shows an advantage over a real plain session, and the difference between the two arms is what screening costs.
ranked_moves.why: The owner's question is comparative, and nothing planned answers it: every existing or planned probe measures a dossier against itself, against pixels or against synthetic shapes. Under the rubric a dimension with no measurement cannot pass 60, and this one instrument also puts numbers on comprehension, claim precision and cost.

[Inferred] that a plain session wins on speed and reach; its time has not been measured.

ranked_moves.title: Settle coverage before prose: a mechanical coverage pre-check and a coverage plan, so fidelity review judges truth only
ranked_moves.relation: new for the pre-check; its replay over stored runs completes syzygy-fnry.21 (classify why first drafts fail); the plan sharpens Q8's outline (syzygy-3efd.50)
ranked_moves.prereq: none for slice 1
ranked_moves.what: Once the independent inventory exists, `check` lists every inventory entry that no draft block cites near (same path, overlapping lines), by entry identifier and path only, never the entry's text, so the inventory stays independent. The author represents each one or records a justified omission, the same two outcomes the reviewer uses today. Next, Syzygy builds a coverage plan from the inventory: each entry assigned to a page and section, deferred to a deep dive, or omitted with a reason, under the page budget. The author drafts against the plan, check verifies the assignments, and the fidelity review's brief narrows to one question: is each claim true to its citation?
ranked_moves.why: Most review failures are bookkeeping, not falsehood, and each one costs a full review round. Removing them is the largest single saving available, and it frees the author's attention for writing.
ranked_moves.basis: [Observed] fidelity verdicts across six stored runs: 20 not ready of 27. [Observed] of 134 blocking findings, 63 are about inventory coverage and 7 say a cited span does not support its claim (lane scripts over reviews/fidelity-verdict-*.json). [Observed] on first verdicts 20 to 42 of 46 to 66 inventory entries were not represented in five runs. [Observed] newest run: 5 minutes of authoring, about 28 of 34 minutes in review rounds.

S2: the review step waits until every listed entry has an outcome
S3: the coverage plan record and its check; the fidelity brief narrowed

ranked_moves.title: Never review the same bytes twice: an unchanged-packet stop, review of only what changed, and a labelled fast draft
ranked_moves.relation: sharpens P15 by using the same block digests between review rounds; narrows P1 (syzygy-fnry.1, design-review every checked revision): every revision is still rendered and reviewed, but a page whose rendered bytes are unchanged keeps the verdict reached over those bytes; the fast draft is new
ranked_moves.prereq: stable block identifiers across revisions (present in the draft schema)
ranked_moves.what: Three rules. A review is not dispatched when its packet digest equals the previous round's; the record says the previous verdict stands. After the first round a fidelity packet carries only blocks whose text, citations or label changed, the inventory entries still open, and the previous round's open findings; unchanged supported blocks carry their verdict forward with the digest it was reached over, and a full re-review runs every third round so carried verdicts cannot drift. A design packet after the first round carries only pages whose rendered bytes changed, plus the landing page. Separately, a fast mode: one author session, the deterministic layers and check, no inventory and no review, with a banner on every page that says so, a tally showing nothing reviewed, and no way to promote it except a full re-run.
ranked_moves.why: Whole review rounds have bought nothing, and every round pays for the whole draft. A review binds to bytes, so carrying a verdict by digest is honest. An owner looking at a new repository often wants its shape in minutes, and an honest label makes that safe.
ranked_moves.basis: [Observed] consecutive identical fidelity verdicts five times across four runs. [Observed] fidelity packets stay 348 to 413 KB within the newest run and design packets are 3.1 to 5.2 MB each (lane script review_economy.py). [Observed] packages/polaris-dossier/src/review-packet.ts builds a whole packet every round.
slices: S1: the unchanged-packet stop
S2: fidelity packets of changed blocks with carried verdict rows and a full re-review every third round
S3: design packets by rendered page digest
S4: the fast mode, its banner and its record flag

ranked_moves.title: An editor session fenced by check, and house style taught by example
ranked_moves.relation: new for the operator-agent loop: it ports the Edit stage that only the parked provider pipeline has; pairs with R5 (review only changed blocks)
ranked_moves.prereq: none
ranked_moves.what: After the first draft passes check, a fresh editor session gets the draft, the rendered pages and the house style. It never gets the repository. It returns changes to wording, order within a section, and merging or splitting of blocks. Check refuses any change to a citation, label, quotation, judgement mark, figure element or Unknown, by comparing each block's claim ledger before and after, and advises when a rewrite introduces an identifier or number not in the block's cited spans. The author accepts or rejects each change. House style becomes a versioned data file of twelve to twenty before-and-after pairs over a fictional project, each tagged with the habit it fixes; the author's and editor's briefs carry the pairs in place of the prose rules now spread over two parts of the brief, which shortens the brief.
ranked_moves.why: One session cannot hold 4,910 words of rules about evidence and also write well. A separate editor can only change how claims read, never what they claim, because check fences it, so voice can improve without risk to truth. Models follow examples more reliably than abstract rules.

[Observed] packages/polaris-dossier/src/brief.ts:54: voice rules are open to no mechanical check. [Observed] session roles are author, inventory and review only (packages/polaris-dossier/src/session-handover.ts); docs/polaris-generation/AUTHORING.md:122-128 defines an Edit stage for the provider pipeline alone.

ranked_moves.title: Quotations as typeset evidence, a thesis line per section, and a prose ledger that describes and never gates
ranked_moves.relation: extends P8 (syzygy-fnry.8, free quotation lead-ins) and syzygy-fnry.13 (clean-text quotation display) with a typeset element; adds a thesis field to Q8; adds prose measures to Q11's stored per-page reading ledger (syzygy-3efd.21) with a rule about who sees them
ranked_moves.prereq: Q11's ledger slice for storage
ranked_moves.what: A quotation the project states becomes its own element: a pull quote set with its file and lines as attribution, attached to the sentence it supports. The formula 'The project states:' leaves the prose; the author writes its own sentence and attaches the quotation as support, and check still verifies the span. Each section gains a one-sentence thesis the renderer sets as its opening. Each run stores model-free prose measures per page (sentence-length spread, apparatus phrases, quotation lead-ins, identifiers per hundred words, whether the opening is an answer, examples and numbers per section, counts of judgements and worth-knowing marks). They appear on the review report and go to the editor and the design reviewer, compared with the previous run. They are never shown to the author and never set readiness.
ranked_moves.why: The quotation formula is the largest single source of stilted prose and of the longest sentences, and it hides the most important claims behind boilerplate. Measures are useful for seeing trends and harmful as targets, so who sees them is part of the design.
ranked_moves.basis: [Observed] nine uses of 'The project states:' in 2,272 words; the three longest sentences (63, 49, 42 words) each open with a quotation and splice in another claim (lane script over the newest draft). [Observed] sentence mechanics are otherwise sound: mean 16.7 words, 90th percentile 27. [Observed] apparatus phrases fell from 57 to 10 between two runs and nothing recorded it.

ranked_moves.title: Ask for insight by name: worth-knowing marks, comparison under a label, and length earned by evidence
ranked_moves.relation: extends P8 (syzygy-fnry.8, a cited judgement per Pole) with comparison under a label and the worth-knowing mark; changes the length rules that Q8's depths and Q10's size tiers make safe to change
ranked_moves.prereq: none from the owner: under VIS-4 as amended by D10 this is an agent adoption, recorded as a row in AGENT-ADOPTIONS.md with its revert command; the owner may veto it. The present rule (a comparison only as quotation) was the owner's trade-off; the adoption row says so and names what changes. Q8's depth slice comes before the length change
ranked_moves.what: Three changes to what the author is asked for. Each Pole carries one to three blocks marked worth knowing: a cited fact an engineer new to the project would not guess from its category, shown as a distinct callout near the top; the inventory session gets the same request, so missing ones surface as coverage gaps. A labelled judgement may compare the project's choice with a named, widely known alternative when it cites the project's own mechanism as its premise and marks the alternative's property as general knowledge and Inferred; it renders as a 'Compared with' aside and never as the maintainers' claim. The flat limits of 300 words per section and three deep dives give way to budgets the evidence earns: a deep dive for each mechanism whose blocks cite at least eight distinct spans in two files, capped by the repository's size tier, and section length that scales with supported claims; check advises a Pole with fewer than three choices or trade-offs on record.
ranked_moves.why: Depth comes from naming the non-obvious, and nothing in the brief asks for it. 'Why this and not the obvious alternative' is the insight a newcomer most wants and a plain session gives freely; forbidding it outright costs depth without buying truth, because the label already carries the state. The limits were a cure for an overlong overview that reading depths now solve.

ranked_moves.title: The why from what maintainers wrote: tests as intent, rough-edge markers, release notes as a timeline, and a rationale scout
ranked_moves.relation: new derived content for Q2's structure record and Q9's pack recognizers. Slice 3 builds run 4's retained tag-and-changelog timeline idea. The scout sharpens P10
ranked_moves.prereq: Q2's structure record (syzygy-3efd.16) for the unit mapping. Root changelog and release-note files and test files in the listed extensions are already admitted by the present policy; only nested changelogs and unlisted extensions need the wider policy (syzygy-3efd.24)
ranked_moves.what: Three deterministic harvests over admitted files, each a derived table. Test names per framework, mapped to units: a Pole shows 'what the tests pin down' and the author may cite a test name as evidence that a behaviour is intended. Markers: TODO, FIXME, deprecation notices and issue references, each a verified line, giving per-unit counts and a 'rough edges and what is going away' page; an issue reference is Observed as a reference and its content is Unknown, because trackers are outside the clone. ranked_moves.title: History as its own screened class: churn, age and hidden coupling derived; commit messages screened as content
ranked_moves.relation: builds run 4's retained full-history idea (and run 3's history mining) by splitting metadata from message content
ranked_moves.prereq: none from the owner: under VIS-4 as amended by D10 this is an agent adoption, recorded as a row in AGENT-ADOPTIONS.md with its revert command; the owner may veto it, because acquisition form and classification are screening policy within SEC-5. Two limits keep it there: commit messages pass the unchanged secret detectors and fail closed, and author identity is dropped at ingestion and never stored. A successor source policy and a change to the acquisition form carry it
ranked_moves.what: Two levels. Metadata only: a history fetch bounded by count or date keeps commit identifiers, dates, parent links and changed paths, and drops author identity and message text at ingestion. From it Syzygy derives churn per unit, age of last change, an age for every cited span ('unchanged since 2019'), and pairs of files that change together yet share no declared or import link, drawn as a hidden-coupling figure. Messages: commit message text becomes a content class that passes the same secret screening as files; the author may quote a message that states a reason, verified like any quotation, and must label any reading of it Inferred. Authorship stays out of both levels.
ranked_moves.why: Where a project is still moving, what is stable, which parts are secretly entangled, and why a design changed: no reading of the current tree can give these, and they are what a senior engineer tells a newcomer first.
ranked_moves.basis: [Observed] packages/polaris-dossier/src/clone-shape.ts:20: the clone holds exactly the pinned commit. [Observed] no production module reads commits, messages or blame. [Observed] .syzygy/governance/policies/POLARIS-DOSSIER-DECLARED-SOURCE-POLICY-v1.json:79-80 lists work-history as never classified. [Inferred] the size of the gain: no dossier has ever cited history.
slices: S1: the successor policy adopted; bounded metadata-only acquisition with identity dropped; churn and age per unit
S2: age on each citation; a per-file timeline on source pages
S3: the hidden-coupling figure, filtered against derived links
S4: screened commit messages as quotable rationale, fail closed

ranked_moves.title: One surface made by one hand: role-named tokens with a lint, colour with two jobs, one shape vocabulary, and a specimen sitting
ranked_moves.relation: extends Q6's figure kinds and Q7's element types with one shape vocabulary; legend generation is Q3 slice 1's (syzygy-3efd.17) and is reused, not rebuilt; builds run 3's retained type-scale idea; new: the token module, the lint and the specimen sitting
ranked_moves.prereq: none; the sitting is optional and the bar's defaults apply until it happens
ranked_moves.what: One module owns every dossier style value by role: a modular type scale, line heights, a four-pixel spacing grid, a reading measure, two radii, and colour roles. Nothing is named after a hue or a typeface. The stylesheet is generated from it, and a test fails on any size, colour or spacing that is not a token. One panel style is kept for figures; emphasis elsewhere uses weight and a rule, not a box. Colour does two jobs only: which Pole something belongs to, and its evidence state; colour by list position goes. Every figure kind draws from one shape vocabulary keyed by element type (a store is a cylinder, an external system a dashed frame), and each figure's legend is generated from the shapes it uses. Taste is settled once: the renderer produces a specimen (the stored Redis overview and one Pole) in three token sets that differ only in typeface pairing, scale ratio, default theme and accent family, the owner picks one in a single sitting, and the pick becomes the default.
ranked_moves.why: A document is trusted on sight when it looks made by one hand. Today's sheet is a stack of fixes that cannot stay consistent, and each review round produces new spacing notes. A single sitting spends the owner's taste where only the owner can decide and nowhere else.
ranked_moves.basis: [Observed] 23 distinct font sizes in three units, 7 radii and 31 one-pixel borders in the dossier stylesheet (lane script over the newest site). ranked_moves.what: A refresh run names a base run. Derived layers, screening verdicts, quotation verifications and inventory entries are stored by the digests of the blobs they read and reused where those are unchanged, each naming the run it came from; model-written prose is never reused silently. Most claims about a mature repository survive a release, and comparing cited bytes is something Syzygy already does to verify them. A returning reader's real question is what to re-learn.

ranked_moves.title: Losses become work: every benchmark dimension Polaris loses files a bounded repair, and the win rule tightens
ranked_moves.relation: new; closes the loop on R1 and R16 the way Q11 closes it for figures
ranked_moves.prereq: R1 slice 3 and R16 slice 3
ranked_moves.what: After each corpus pass, a script reads the benchmark records and, for each dimension and repository where the dossier scored below the plain arm, files one repair bead naming the questions or depth items lost, the pages that should have answered them, and the likely cause class (coverage, depth, prose, figure, navigation), from a fixed list. The win rule's ten percent tolerance on comprehension and depth becomes 'not worse' after two passes, and 'better on at least one of the two' after four. The report of each pass leads with losses. Losses are merged by cause class across repositories before filing, and a pass files at most five repair packets, largest loss first; the rest stay in the loss report. The loop also chases the ceiling: when the dossier falls below the maintainer-documentation arm on the depth list by more than a margin fixed in the protocol, that gap files a repair too, inside the same cap of five.
ranked_moves.why: A benchmark only measures. An advantage over a plain session has to be built, and the cheapest way to find what to build is to ask where the plain session won.

ranked_moves.title: People in the loop: a small human panel calibrates every model-graded measure
ranked_moves.relation: new; calibrates R1's grader, R17's raters and P7's reader

why: It sends files the policy cannot classify, which today are 'indeterminate … excluded from reading and from egress (fail closed)' (policy :257). RFC5-14 reserves exactly that to the owner: 'A change that would let content the secret-detection policy matches, or cannot classify, reach a provider is the owner's decision (SEC-5)'.

'Minus only the files the unchanged secret detectors flag' also drops two screens that are not detectors: the denied-path rule (`.env`, `credentials.json`, `secrets.json`, `id_rsa`, `.pem`, `.key`, `.p12`, `.pfx`; policy :469-486) and the active-content and private-repository rules. A `.env` or `.pem` whose secret no regular expression matches would be sent. VIS-4's owner class 2 covers 'anything that would weaken secret detection or SEC-5's fail-closed rule, or let a secret be … sent'.
Relabelling every unclassifiable file into a catch-all class is the fail-closed rule removed by another name, not a classification decision.
faults.fix: Either put the arm to the owner, or redefine it as 'the whole clone minus denied paths, detector matches and active content, each unclassifiable file placed in a named class by an explicit rule, public repositories only'. units.gap: A dossier costs 30 to 81 minutes of wall time from first prompt to last step across six stored runs. It uses four model sessions (author, inventory, fidelity, design), three to seven draft revisions, and about a dozen operator touches. Its token cost is unknown because usage is self-reported at close and was not recorded on the newest run. Fidelity review is where the time goes. units.gap: Across the six run-5 units, three systemic causes recur. (1) One session is asked to do every job at once. A single author holds 4,910 words of brief, 85% of it about what may be claimed, and must explore, cover every inventory entry, stay under 300 words per section, and write well. Fidelity review then judges truth and coverage bookkeeping together. Result: flat, formula-bound prose (prose), one choice and one trade-off for all of Redis (insight-depth), and 20 of 27 fidelity verdicts not-ready, mostly over coverage (economy). (2) The rules guard against error by forbidding whole kinds of content rather than by labelling them. History is never classified, comparisons may only be quoted, and an unstated advantage is forbidden even as Inferred. The labels that doctrine already provides (Inferred, judgement) go unused, at 0 and 0 in the newest draft. This buys truth at the cost of the 'why' a newcomer wants and a vanilla session supplies freely. (3) Nothing is measured against anything outside the dossier. There is no vanilla arm, no stored reader result, no token cost, no run-over-run ledger, no first-screen assertion and no CSS census, so dimensions 5 to 8 cannot score above 60 under the rubric however good the work is. units.gap: Nothing in the repository can compare a dossier with a plain session today. The reader-test engine exists but has one implementation, a scripted port that returns answers fixed in advance, and it records accuracy as 'not-evaluated'. proposals.title: A pre-registered vanilla-arm benchmark that Polaris can lose
proposals.what: Three arms per repository: (A) a Polaris dossier; (B) one plain session with the same model, clone, sandbox and wall-clock cap, given a fixed published prompt ('Explain this repository to a newly hired engineer: why it exists, how it works, its key trade-offs; include diagrams as Mermaid') and three fixed scripted follow-ups; (C) the maintainers' own site, as a ceiling. Before any generation, freeze per repository: the seven TARGETS questions; a depth rubric of 10-20 non-obvious facts and trade-offs drawn from maintainer docs, ADRs and changelogs by a session that never sees A or B (CodeWikiBench-style); and five reader tasks ('where would I change X'). Measurements: (1) claim accuracy, sampling 40 claims per arm, each judged by a verifier session holding the clone with the arm identity hidden, plus V2's mechanical check on any file:line either arm gives; (2) comprehension, with fresh readers answering the frozen questions from the rendered arm only, graded against the frozen key; (3) depth, as rubric items covered; (4) task success; (5) figures, as count plus the run-4 pixel round-trip; (6) cost: tokens, wall time, operator minutes. Blinding: both arms are rendered to the same neutral HTML shell, with Polaris's apparatus folded and B's file references kept, so graders see content, not chrome. Pre-registered win rule: Polaris wins only if its accuracy error rate is at most half of B's AND its comprehension and depth scores are not lower by more than 10% AND its cost is within a stated multiple (proposed: 10x tokens, 5x wall time). Anything else is published as a loss, with the dimensions named.
proposals.why: Rubric dimension 7 cannot score above 60 without a measurement, and the owner's question ('a substantial improvement over vanilla sessions?') has no answer today. units.framing: The stored runs show where the money goes. Most fidelity rounds fail on one predictable thing: a first draft that leaves out much of the independent inventory. proposals.title: A mechanical coverage pre-check before fidelity: name the inventory entries the draft never touches
proposals.what: Once the inventory has run, `check` computes, for each inventory entry, whether any draft claim block cites a span that overlaps that entry's cited spans (same path, overlapping line range), or names the entry's path. Entries with no overlap are listed to the author as advice, by entry id and path only: 'inventory entry inv-23 (src/aof.c:1210-1288) has no draft block citing it'. The entry's claim text is never shown, so the author must read the source and decide, which keeps the inventory independent. The author represents each entry or records a justified omission, the same dispositions the reviewer uses. Fidelity then reviews a draft whose obvious coverage gaps are already closed. The pre-check never sets readiness; the reviewer still judges coverage.
proposals.why: Coverage omissions are the largest repeated cause of not-ready verdicts, and a citation overlap catches most of them for nothing. Each avoided fidelity round saves a review of 280 to 770 KB plus an author revision. It also moves the 'unsupported' counts on first verdicts (38/66 typical) toward the 12/92 the best run reached.
proposals.basis: VIS-2 (a gap shown, never hidden); the independence of the inventory session is preserved because only ids and paths cross
proposals.relation_to_known: New. It sits upstream of the fidelity review that P1-P15 assume.

proposals.title: Review only what changed, and never review the same bytes twice
proposals.what: Two rules. (1) A packet digest gate: the supervisor refuses to dispatch a review whose packet digest equals the previous round's, and records 'unchanged, previous verdict stands'. (2) Delta packets: after round 0, a fidelity packet carries the blocks whose text, citations or label changed (keyed by block id and its content digest), the inventory entries whose disposition was open, and the previous verdict's open findings. Unchanged supported blocks carry forward their 'supported' verdict with the digest it was reached over, and the verdict file records which rows were carried and from which round. A design packet after round 0 carries only pages whose rendered bytes changed, plus the landing page always. A full re-review happens on demand or every Nth round (proposed: 3), so carry-forward cannot drift indefinitely.
proposals.why: Five consecutive identical verdicts mean whole rounds bought nothing. Packets that stay at 90-100% of their first size mean every round pays for the whole draft. Delta review is the standard incremental-build move, and digest-keyed carry-forward keeps it honest under rule 10 (a review binds to bytes).
proposals.basis: VIS-2 and the rule-10 discipline already used across the repository: a verdict is bound to the bytes it read, so a carried verdict names its digest
proposals.relation_to_known: Sharpens P15 (regeneration and claim diff) by applying the same block digests inside one run, between review rounds.
proposals.prereq: Stable block ids across revisions (already present in draft-schema.ts)
integration_points: packages/polaris-dossier/src/review-verdict.ts (carried rows with carried-from-round and digest fields)

proposals.title: A labelled fast draft, and a cache keyed by blob digest across runs
proposals.what: Fast mode: one author session, the deterministic layers (census, run-4's derived structure, W1-W3 tables) and `check`, but no inventory and no reviews. Every page carries a banner 'Draft — not reviewed: no independent inventory, no fidelity or design review', the tally ribbon shows reviewed=0, and the run record marks the run fast. Fast mode cannot be promoted, only re-run full. Cache: derived layers, screening verdicts, quotation verifications and inventory entries are stored by the blob digests they read. A run at a new commit reuses any whose blobs are unchanged and recomputes the rest. A reused inventory entry or verification names the run it came from. units.framing: A newcomer can get the what from the code. A manifesto's value is the why: why this design, what it replaced, what it costs, what is fragile, what is on its way out. That knowledge sits in places the dossier never reads: tests (intent the maintainers made executable), release notes and changelogs (decisions in time order), in-code markers (TODO, FIXME, deprecations, issue references), and git history (churn, age, files that change together, commit messages). The lens sorts these by what Syzygy can derive deterministically as Observed (names, counts, dates, co-change), what it can verify as a quotation (Observed text whose meaning is the author's Inferred reading), and what needs a new acquisition or a new content class. History is the one that needs an owner decision.

A Pole page gets a 'What the tests pin down' strip: the 5-8 test names whose words overlap that Pole's glossary terms, each linking to its line, plus a count ('214 tests cover the persistence unit'). proposals.title: In-code rationale markers: debt, deprecations and issue references as a derived 'rough edges' layer
proposals.what: A deterministic lexical scan over admitted blobs, never comment meaning. It finds TODO, FIXME, HACK and XXX markers; deprecation markers (`@deprecated`, `#[deprecated]`, `DeprecationWarning`, `[Obsolete]`, `// Deprecated:` in Go, 'deprecated since' and 'Deprecated' headings in changelogs); and issue or PR references (`#1234` in comments, `GH-1234`, URLs to issue trackers). Each hit is a derived row: kind, path, line, marker text up to the line end, which is a verified quotation, and unit. Rendered output: per-unit counts on atlas cards ('persistence: 12 TODO · 3 deprecated APIs'), a 'Rough edges and what is going away' reference page, and per-Pole callouts when a Pole's cited files carry deprecations. Issue references are Observed as references. Their content is Unknown, because issue trackers are outside the clone and fetching them is egress.
proposals.why: This is the non-obvious knowledge a senior engineer gives a newcomer first ('don't build on that, it's deprecated'; 'that module is held together with TODOs'), and Syzygy can derive it exactly. It also gives the trade-offs topic evidence the maintainers themselves wrote.
proposals.basis: VIS-2 and the Observed definition; brief topic `mechanisms-and-trade-offs` (brief.ts:51) asks for limits and costs
proposals.relation_to_known: New. It feeds run-4 Q10's atlas cards and Q3's tally vocabulary.

proposals.title: Release notes and changelogs as the decision record in time order
proposals.what: A changelog recognizer covers the Keep a Changelog headings, `## [x.y.z] - date`, release-notes files such as `00-RELEASENOTES`, `HISTORY.*`, `NEWS` and `docs/releases/*`, and per-version sections. It derives a version timeline (Observed: version, date where stated, line range) and classifies entries by heading only (Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security), never by reading. The author may then write 'how it got here' claims that quote entries containing a stated reason. A brief rule asks for at least one per major mechanism where the notes state one. These render as dated cards on a timeline figure (run-4 Q6 timeline kind) and as 'since version X' badges beside the mechanisms they changed.
proposals.why: Release notes are where maintainers say why a design changed ('replaced X because Y'). Redis's notes were cited only as a description of what changed, never as rationale. A time axis is also one of the most orienting figures a newcomer can get.
proposals.basis: VIS-3 (digestible to a newcomer); AUTHORING.md 'A comparison, timeline or workflow may explain one project better than a component map'
proposals.relation_to_known: Sharpens run-4's unranked tag-timeline idea (I1-M5) into a decision record. It uses Q6's timeline kind.
proposals.prereq: Q6 timeline kind for the figure; none for the derived table

proposals.title: History as its own consented class: churn, age and hidden coupling derived as Observed; commit messages screened as content
proposals.what: There are two acquisition levels. Level H1, metadata only: a history fetch bounded by count or date (for example the last 2,000 commits or 3 years) that keeps commit ids, dates, parent links and changed paths, and drops author identity and message bodies at ingestion. From it Syzygy derives churn per file and unit, last-change age, a co-change matrix (pairs of files that change together more than a stated threshold and share no derived import or manifest edge, the 'hidden coupling' figure), and an age per cited span (each citation shows 'unchanged since 2019-04'). All of these are counts and dates over git objects, so they are Observed by derivation. Level H2, commit messages: message bodies become a content class that runs through the same secret screening as files. The author may quote a message that states a reason, verified like any quotation, and must label any reading of it Inferred. Authorship stays out of both levels unless the owner decides otherwise.
proposals.why: Churn, age and coupling are the non-obvious facts no reading of the current tree can give: where the project is still moving, what is stable, which parts are secretly entangled. Commit messages are the richest rationale source in most repositories. Rubric dimension 5 gains most here.
proposals.basis: Observed by derivation under trust-and-evidence's own definition, so no doctrine change. It does stretch the spec-level acquisition form (one commit, clone-shape.ts:20) and adds a content class. Under D10 that makes it an owner question on two counts: commit messages can carry secrets, and authorship is personal data. [Inferred: if the owner reads SEC-2 consent as covering only the tree at the pinned commit, this becomes vision-extending and needs a SEC-2 amendment.]
proposals.relation_to_known: Supersedes run-3's retained 'history mining' (I2-M3) and run-4's parked full-history tier. Splits metadata (H1) from content (H2).
proposals.prereq: Owner decision: whether a dossier run may fetch bounded history (H1), and whether commit messages are an admitted, screened class (H2); authorship stays out by default. Then a spec change to the acquisition form (dossier-declared-source-model / F-3 clone shape).

units.framing: The measurement surprised this lens. Sentence mechanics are no longer the problem. In the newest Redis draft sentences average 16.7 words (p90 27), hedges and passives are rare, every section opens with an answer, and apparatus fell from 57 phrases to 10 between run d9411d26 and the newest run 658f2f90. A mechanical style checker would mostly confirm what is already fine, and would teach the author to write to it. What the prose lacks is substance and voice: 2,100 words for all of Redis, zero judgements, and no sentence a senior engineer would underline as 'I didn't know that'. So this lens spends its moves on asking for insight, editing as a separate act, and style taught by example. Metrics stay descriptive and out of the author's sight.

proposals.title: An editor session: one fresh reader-writer who reads the checked draft as an argument and returns block diffs
proposals.what: After the first draft passes `check`, and before the fidelity review, a fresh editor session receives the draft, the rendered pages (or P6 screenshots once they exist), the house style (VO2) and the prose ledger (VO4). It never receives the clone. It returns a block-level diff: rewritten text for blocks, reordering within a section, and merges or splits of blocks. It may not change any citation, label, quotation span, judgement mark, figure element or Unknown. `check` refuses a diff that does, mechanically, by comparing every claim block's citation set, label and quotation list before and after. It also refuses a rewrite that introduces a new identifier or number absent from the block's cited spans; this is lexical and advisory at first. The author then accepts or rejects each diff hunk, and the result is a new draft revision. Fidelity reviews only rewritten blocks (economy E2).
proposals.why: Writing and editing are different jobs. The author spends its attention on evidence, so the prose is correct but flat. A separate editor can only improve how claims read, never what they claim, because the check fences it. This is the cheapest route to voice that cannot cost truth.
proposals.basis: VIS-1 (comprehension through presentation, never content: 'simplifying presentation, never content'); AUTHORING.md Edit stage
proposals.relation_to_known: New for the operator-agent loop. It ports AUTHORING.md's Edit stage, which only the parked provider pipeline has. It pairs with economy E2 (review only changed blocks).

proposals.title: House style as data: exemplar pairs, not more rules
proposals.what: A versioned `house-style.json` of 12-20 before-and-after pairs, each tagged with the habit it fixes: apparatus ('Every entry here is the project's own wording, quoted from its files' becomes a direct claim); claim-first ('X buys A by B and pays for it in C'); hand-off causality ('so that …'); naming the alternative a design rejects, when the sources name it; one concrete number or example per abstraction; and a judgement with its premise. Pairs are Syzygy-written and project-neutral, built over a fictional project, so a brief carries no other project's content and no copyrighted prose. The author brief and the editor brief (VO1) carry them in place of the prose habits currently spread across VOICE_RULES and READABILITY_GUIDANCE. That trims the brief rather than adding to it. The V1 benchmark A/B-tests a house-style version before it becomes the default.
proposals.why: Models imitate examples far more reliably than they follow abstract rules, and today's voice guidance is numbered rules spread across two blocks of brief text (brief.ts:55-61 and :82-90). Keeping style as data makes it versioned, reviewable and testable, like run-4's shape packs.

proposals.title: Ask for insight by name: a 'worth knowing' mark per Pole
proposals.what: The brief asks each Pole for one to three blocks marked `worthKnowing: true`: a cited fact a competent engineer new to this project would not guess from its category alone. Examples of the shape: 'writes are durable only after the next fsync, by default once a second', or 'the event loop is single-threaded, but I/O threads parse and write'. They render as a distinct 'Worth knowing' callout near the top of the Pole. `check` counts them as advice. The V1 benchmark's frozen depth rubric scores whether they match what maintainers and experts flag. The independent inventory session gets the same request, so 'worth knowing' items the draft lacks show up as coverage gaps, as other inventory entries do.
proposals.why: Depth does not come from longer prose. It comes from naming the non-obvious, and nothing in today's brief asks for it. Making it a marked element gives readers the thing vanilla sessions do well (a sharp 'gotcha') and gives the benchmark a population to score.
proposals.basis: VIS-3; the brief's mechanisms-and-trade-offs topic (brief.ts:51); rubric dimension 5
proposals.relation_to_known: New. It complements P8 (judgements with receipts): a worth-knowing block is a cited fact, not a judgement.

proposals.title: A prose ledger that describes and never gates, kept out of the author's sight
proposals.what: Each run stores the model-free prose metrics per page and per section: the sentence-length distribution, hedge and passive rates, apparatus phrases, quotation lead-ins, identifier density, opening-is-an-answer (first sentence declarative and free of apparatus), concreteness (numbers, code excerpts and examples per section), and counts of judgements and worth-knowing blocks. The ledger is shown on the review report, diffed against the previous run of the same repository, and handed to the editor session (VO1) and the design reviewer. It is never in `check` output to the author, and it never sets readiness. Only extreme outliers raise a design-review prompt: p90 over 35 words, or more than 3 apparatus phrases per 1,000 words.
proposals.why: Metrics are useful to see trends (the apparatus collapse above was invisible until measured) and dangerous as targets. Keeping them out of the author loop is the 'avoid writing to the checker' rule made structural.
proposals.basis: VIS-2 (measure what is known); AUTHORING.md 'neither a word quota nor an exhaustive catalog is the objective'
proposals.relation_to_known: Sharpens run-4 Q11's stored reading ledger with a prose metric set and an explicit rule about who may see it.
